source.title: AI4AI-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Algorithmic Design for Recursive Self-Improvement

findings.mechanism: Separate run-side optimization from edits that change the learning algorithm; use measurement rigs and failure-mechanism diagnosis before algorithmic intervention.
quantitative_evidence: Across 29 configurations of 6 systems on 10 frozen research repositories, mean normalized score was 0.166 and best mean was 0.250.
Among 263 classifiable changed submissions, 46.4% touched the learning side and 53.6% stayed run-side only.
Learning-side submissions averaged 0.226 versus 0.126 for run-side-only submissions, a 0.100 gap with standard error 0.022; authors explicitly caution this is observational rather than causal.

Increasing reasoning effort raised the share of submissions touching the learning algorithm from 8% to 64% and mean score from 0.094 to 0.196, while median task exploration cost rose from $1.69 to $34.60.

Successful examples built local measurement/diagnostic machinery before intervention; one Model Soup submission reduced proxy evaluation from about 190 s to 0.38 s (~500x) and used it to compare alternatives, while an OWL submission reduced perplexity from 53.4 to just over 13 after diagnosing a failure mode and changing the learning pipeline.
findings.evidence_scope: Strong new benchmark evidence about where agent search effort lands and how outcomes correlate with intervention layer. The learning-side versus run-side score difference is not randomized causal evidence; do not treat it as proof that any learning-side edit will improve O.
findings.o_relevance: Add intervention-layer coverage and measurement-first diagnostics as explicit dimensions when evaluating O self-improvement proposals. A useful test is whether O's search is mostly tuning execution/scaffolding rather than trying falsifiable learning-rule changes when the task actually permits them.
findings.novelty: Paper appeared after the previous O continuity checkpoint and was absent from prior worker state.

findings.mechanism: Persistent self-improvement requires explicit Plan/Render/Route/Gate/Close pathways, not merely storing state. Measure write/read/update receipts and matched persistence-on/off behavior.
quantitative_evidence: 26 scenarios and 204 episodes use ordered fresh-session sequences with matched persistence-on/off conditions.

Across tested base models, persistence produced positive overall gaps in the reported Hermes framework: GLM-5.1 +0.20, Kimi K2.6 +0.17, DeepSeek-V4-Pro +0.17, MiniMax-M2.7 +0.13, GPT-5.4 +0.24, Claude Sonnet 4.6 +0.20, Claude Opus 4.6 +0.19.
Single-mechanism ablations on MiniMax show retrieval gate E4 had the largest single overall gap (+0.17); closeout E5 had the strongest single Update gap (+0.16); full Hermes+ reached Update +0.24.

Focused procedural leave-one-out results show non-monotonic interactions: full Hermes+ +0.085, without E2 memory binding +0.108, without E5 closeout +0.042. Thus adding a component can help one capability while hurting another.
Hermes+ versus Hermes overall was +0.15 versus +0.13, but the authors report that the +0.02 difference is smaller than run-to-run variation; transfer was also non-uniform across model families.
findings.evidence_scope: Matched benchmark design with mechanism telemetry, but authors explicitly do not claim causal proof. Aggregate Hermes+ superiority is not established beyond run variance; component effects interact and can reverse by capability/model.
findings.o_relevance: Directly relevant to O's Context Kernel: evaluate not only context availability but whether relevant state is rendered, routed, consulted before action, and flushed after correction. Preserve O's existing anti-overgeneralization rule because some components regress particular capabilities.
findings.novelty: Very recent benchmark and not present in prior worker state.

source.title: Darwin Godel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents

findings.mechanism: Keep an open archive of diverse self-modified agents/stepping stones instead of greedy single-lineage hill-climbing.
quantitative_evidence: Reported table: DGM 50.0% SWE-bench and 38.0% Polyglot subset; without open-ended exploration 23.0% and 14.0%; without self-improvement 39.0% and 28.0%; greedy 39.7% and 30.0%.
Three Polyglot DGM runs averaged 40.7% with standard deviation 2.3% on the paper's evaluated subset.
Estimated one DGM SWE-bench run cost about $22,000 versus about $10,000 for baseline runs.
findings.evidence_scope: Strong scaffold-level ablations in coding domains, but expensive, domain-specific, and the outer exploration process itself is fixed rather than recursively self-modified.
findings.o_relevance: Supports preserving diverse stepping stones/branches when testing self-modifications rather than committing only to the current best lineage. Cost makes direct reproduction unattractive unless a cheaper matched proxy is available.

source.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning

findings.mechanism: Use rich trajectory-level natural-language feedback to make targeted prompt mutations, while preserving a Pareto frontier of complementary candidates instead of collapsing experience to scalar reward/best-only selection.
quantitative_evidence: Across six tasks in the final ICLR abstract, GEPA outperforms GRPO by 6 percentage points on average and up to 19 points while using up to 35x fewer rollouts.
It also exceeds MIPROv2 by over 10 points, including +12 points on AIME-2025.
findings.evidence_scope: Prompt/system optimization rather than weight-level recursive self-improvement. Headline rollout efficiency depends on comparison accounting and should be verified task-by-task before treating it as a universal compute multiplier.
findings.o_relevance: Candidate for O's self-revision layer: retain diagnostic trajectories and evolve multiple prompt/context-policy candidates using rich failure explanations rather than only scalar task scores.

source.title: MARS: Modular Agent with Reflective Search for Automated AI Research

findings.mechanism: Budget-aware tree search plus comparative reflective memory that transfers lessons across branches.
quantitative_evidence: Official MLE-Bench results list CAIR MARS at 56.0 +/- 1.54 and MARS+ at 62.67 +/- 0.77 under 24-hour Gemini-3-Pro-Preview settings.
The paper reports that 63% of utilized lessons originated from cross-branch transfer.
findings.evidence_scope: MARS to MARS+ is not yet treated here as an isolated ablation of reflective memory; the 63% statistic is provenance of utilized lessons, not causal uplift. The public leaderboard later contains higher-scoring systems, so do not repeat the paper's original SOTA wording as a current ranking claim.
findings.o_relevance: Supports testing cross-branch lesson transfer separately from candidate-archive retention. Needs component ablations before promotion as a causal mechanism.
